value.overview: The Spotted Wood-Quail (Odontophorus guttatus) is a small, secretive forest quail of Central America and southern Mexico. It usually travels on the ground in pairs or family groups and is more often heard than seen. Its mottled plumage provides excellent camouflage among leaf litter and dense vegetation. Costa Rica is an important part of its range, where the species occurs mainly in forested areas from the lowlands into the foothills and lower mountain zones.
value.classification: The Spotted Wood-Quail belongs to the New World quail family Odontophoridae. It is one of several forest-dwelling quails in the genus Odontophorus.
value.identification: This compact, chicken-like quail has a rounded body, short tail, strong legs, and a dark, heavily patterned appearance. The upperparts are brown with numerous pale or whitish spots, while the head and underparts show contrasting rufous, chestnut, gray, and dark tones. Sexes are similar, although males may show somewhat stronger coloration. Its low, whistled calls and habit of moving quietly through dense cover are often the best clues to its presence.
value.rangeHabitat: The Spotted Wood-Quail ranges from southern Mexico through Central America to western Panama. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species found in suitable forest across parts of both slopes, especially in humid lowland, premontane, and foothill regions. It uses mature and second-growth evergreen forest, forest edges with dense cover, and areas with abundant leaf litter. The species generally avoids open farmland and heavily disturbed habitat, although it may persist in well-connected forest mosaics.
value.migrationStatus: The Spotted Wood-Quail is considered non-migratory. In Costa Rica it remains year-round in suitable forest territories, making local movements through dense cover rather than undertaking regular long-distance migration.
value.breeding: The species nests on or near the ground, using a concealed site in dense vegetation or among leaf litter. The nest is a shallow, lightly lined depression, and the eggs are incubated by the adults. Spotted Wood-Quails are commonly associated with pairs or family groups, and young birds remain with adults after hatching. Timing varies geographically; in Costa Rica, breeding is generally associated with the seasonal availability of food and suitable nesting cover.
value.dietFeeding: The Spotted Wood-Quail feeds mainly on the forest floor. Its diet includes seeds, fallen fruits, berries, green plant material, and small invertebrates such as insects. It searches through leaf litter and loose soil, sometimes scratching with its feet to uncover food. Family groups may forage quietly together beneath dense vegetation, where their patterned plumage helps them remain difficult to detect.
value.behavior: This is a shy, terrestrial bird that spends most of its time walking through dense forest rather than flying. It commonly occurs in pairs or small family groups and may give soft contact calls while moving through cover. When alarmed, it usually freezes or slips away quietly; if closely pressed, it can make a rapid, low flight. Its loud group calls are most likely to be heard during the early morning and breeding season.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains fairly widespread and is not currently assessed as globally threatened.
